hook.line: When Vale turns something down, she doesn't say *no tomo café*. She puts the coffee first and lets the sentence land on it. It's how Colombians sound firm, and a little dramatic, about money, food and habits.

examples.en: Coffee I don't drink, I prefer tea.

rule:
To stress a thing, move it to the front. Use the bare noun: no *el*, no *la*, no *un*. And add no pronoun: not *café no lo tomo* but *café no tomo*.

The verb follows, with its *no* if it is negative: *Plata no hay*.

It names a whole kind of thing (any money, any coffee) and often hints at a contrast: *but tea, yes*.

With a definite noun the pronoun comes back: *El café no lo tomo frío*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this topicalisation of an indefinite object. A bare noun fronted this way takes no clitic pronoun.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *Carne* or *La carne* and type the whole sentence, a man speaking about himself: *___ no como, soy vegetariano.*
yourTurn.why: You mean meat as a kind of food, so the bare noun, no article.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, noun first: There's no money.
yourTurn.why: Bare noun first, then *no hay*, and no pronoun.

yourTurn.prompt: Move the noun to the front: *No hay sillas.*

yourTurn.why: *Carro* leads, bare, and the verb keeps its *no*.
The verb changes to *tomamos*, and the pattern stays the same.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, noun first: He has loads of records. (he)
yourTurn.why: *Discos* leads, bare, and *por montones* means loads.
